comments.content: Hi JMG, I've been going through meditations on the geomantic correspondences and I had a question. Is there any indication in the literature you've read of reasons for the house correspondences of the figures? Is it just a matter of copying the house correspondences of their corresponding star signs, moving through the houses in order or is there a pattern apart from that? I'm starting to see a meaningful pattern emerging from the house correspondences of the figures and I'm wondering if anyone else has seen it. If you can answer first I'll tell you the pattern I'm seeing. Thanks.

replies.title: Re: Geomantic House Significance
replies.content: The explanation I've seen derives it from astrology, and from the natural rulers of the 12 houses -- Aries for the 1st, Taurus for the 2nd, and so on. The Aries personality tends to be self-centered, so the 1st has to do with the self; the Taurus personality is possessive, so the 2nd has to do with possessions, and so on.

replies.title: Re: Geomantic House Significance
replies.content:
Here's what I'm seeing in the house correspondences. The figures and their houses trace out the familiar narrative of the hero's journey.

Puer is the protagonist figure projected onto the querent (strong first house) as the central personage in the reading. A legendary hero often begins their journey lacking many social ties (weak seventh house), and may be an orphan or outsider in the setting.

Amissio represents misfortune befalling the hero. Something causes them to lose their home and/or possessions (strong second house) but escape with their life (weak eighth house). This loss may be their call to adventure.

Albus is a mentor who journeys with the hero for a time and teaches them (strong third house) but who cannot accompany the hero the entire way (weak ninth house).

Populus is a town where the hero's never been (string fourth house) or another crowded place where the hero's journey leads. As an outsider here they are of low social status (weak tenth house).

In the example of Star Wars, Puer is Luke Skywalker, Amissio is the death of his aunt and uncle and the destruction of his home, Albus is Obi-Wan Kenobi and Populus is Mos Eisley.

I'm still working through meditations on each correspondence so this is far as I've gotten, I don't want to skip ahead for the sake of discipline in fully exploring each figure in due time. Still, just from looking at the series of figures it's clear that the Cauda/Caput Draconis pair would represent the climax of the story. What do you think of this interpretation? I don't see the hero's journey pattern being applicable to the zodiac signs in the same way, they don't evoke the same kind of specific narrative archetypes to me.

replies.title: Re: Geomantic House Significance
replies.content: Fascinating. I'll want to ponder this, and probably meditate on it.

replies.title: Re: Geomantic House Significance
replies.content:
That is VERY interesting, Anonymous!
I went through Art and Practice of Geomancy and drew the strong figures inside each house, putting the weak figures on the border outside of the House chart. Noting the doubled up strong figures in houses III, IV, V, and VI, and their corresponding doubled-up weak positions in IX, X, XI and XII.
Tentatively, it could be that the hero makes the circuit and ends with Cauda Drac, Via, Fortuna Minor, and Caput Drac, which is (at the end) reminiscent of the wheat stalk held aloft at the end of the Elusinian Mystery. So it may be, not just a hero's journey, but a road map to the Elusynian Mystery.
For sure, a worthy topic for meditation. Thanks for sharing this! I look forward to another post somewhere with your full meditation!

A few weeks ago I had a question about skepticism and doubt, since then some reflections and synchronicities led to a realization. I was starting to read some of the pre-Socratics, who among other things started a shift from mythic to rational thought, and that triggered the strange awareness that my own thinking patterns are inherited from this long history of philosophy. I got the felt sense for a few moments of distance from this inheritance, that it isn’t something absolute or fixed in reality, but it was brought about by these other people in history through education and custom. Maybe a lot of what I have been reading from yourself and other writers over the years finally sunk in a bit more deeply.

It’s a bit disconcerting, I find myself wondering how to work with this. It is kind of like a sense that the intellect isn’t a fundamental frame of reference, it is just something smaller within a bigger frame, and intellectual argument is useful only in certain contexts but often misses the point about something bigger. But I am still grappling with it all.

Is there a way to keep the best of both worlds: the mythic and the rational or are they mutually exclusive? And is it possible for someone with my cultural upbringing to experience the mythic mode of thinking due to the rational baggage?

replies.title: (no subject)
replies.content:
The mythic is the inescapable basis of human thought. You can't get away from it no matter how hard you try. Rational thinking is a rickety structure built atop that foundation, powerful in its way but also limited and fragile. Nor does it exclude mythic thinking. Rationalists are just as quick to think in mythic terms as anyone else -- get them talking about progress, or space travel, or reason itself, and the mythic metaphors come out at once!

The thing you have to overcome isn't reason, it's the myth of reason -- the particular set of mythic narratives that portray reason as the savior of humanity. To overcome them, you simply have to understand that those narratives are just another set of myths. Once you do that, you can use reasoning where it's appropriate and set it aside where it's not.

comments.title: Geomancy Chart – Book Publishing
comments.content:
Hi, JMG. I’ve cast a geomancy chart on a personal question that I am hoping to get a second opinion on, as the question involves a potential long-term commitment of sorts, the matter is rather close to me, and it is not the easiest chart in the world to interpret. Plus - maybe you have cast a chart or two for yourself on this situation in the past.

I cast a chart to the question of “If I write the book that I desire to, will I be able to get it published?

The four mothers are Tristitia (1M), Puella (2M), Populus (3M), and Fortuna Minor (4M).

The court is: Conjunctio (right witness), Fortuna Minor (left witness) and Amissio (judge). Amissio is usually not a great judge figure. However, looking in context, I see Conjunctio reflecting the push-pull situation in my mind – a desire and confidence to write the book but doubts whether a publisher will touch it. And I see Fortuna Minor as a limited-time opportunity from the publisher’s side, and also a possibility that the influence of others may be of help to me. Perhaps the Amissio judge indicates a loss of doubts in my mind (I’d rather have a positive left witness and a negative or neutral right witness than the other way around), in which case the judge is positive. The reconciler is Puella, which I see as a positive sign.

In the house chart, the querent is Tristitia (1st house) and I have identified a dual quesited of the 3rd house figure (signifying books), which is Populus; and the 10th house figure (signifying persons in a position of authority – i.e., the publisher is in this situation), which is Fortuna Minor.

Now, being a yes/no kind of question, my focus has been almost exclusively on the perfection, or denial of perfection, among the querent figure and the two quesited figures in the house chart.

Tristitia – the querent figure – passes to the 6th house, while Fortuna Minor – the figure of the publisher – passes to the 4th house and the 8th house. Populus – the figure of the book – is not duplicated in the chart. Figures in company are not a factor in this chart.

Putting this all together, we have a complex relationship between me and the publisher, as Tristitia in the 6th house forms a trine with Fortuna Minor in the 10th house, as well as two sextiles with Fortuna Minor in the 8th and 4th houses. Meanwhile, Fortuna Minor in the 4th house forms a square with Tristitia in the 1st house. This makes it an overall positive situation, but not without problems.

When factoring in the significator of the book (Populus in the 3rd house), the 4th house Fortuna Minor perfects via conjunction (which is stronger than any aspect), while the 6th house Tristitia forms a square aspect.

To my mind, the key factor is whether or not the publisher likes my book (not whether it likes “me”) and here I see a strong “yes” as the answer due to the conjunction mentioned above, but it may not be a “slam dunk” (well, having never had a book published, I don’t really expect a slam dunk).

I see two possible flies in the ointment: (1) if I add the significators of the querent and the publisher, the figure is Puer which seems contentious to me; and (2) if I look to the 7th house as the significator of contracts, the figure is the rambunctious Rubeus (oh, poop!), which passes to the 11th house conjunct with the Publisher and in sextile to me – so, though there is perfection here it is with just about the worst figure imaginable.

Your thoughts on this chart? Many thanks in advance!

Jaundice Libidinous Earthworm (my nom du jour)

replies.title: Re: Geomancy Chart – Book Publishing
replies.content:
Okay, this is a classic example of extreme overthinking. You asked a yes/no question, you need to start by looking for a yes/no answer. Let's begin with the court. You have one mildly positive witness (Fortuna Minor), one ambivalent witness (Conjunctio), and a negative judge (Amissio). The two witnesses indicate that you have a chance but only if you act quickly and take advantage of an opportunity that will not last long. Amissio says the odds are against you.

The house chart is similar. Publication is a third house question. Yes, you can bring in other houses -- if you're ingenious enough, you can come up with some reason to include every single house in the chart! -- but that muddies the reading and makes accurate predictions impossible. There is no mode of perfection uniting the 1st and 3rd house ruler other than a square from the 6th, which indicates "Maybe, but you'll regret it." Tristitia in the 1st is also the opposite of a good omen.

All the other indications are secondary to these primary indications and need to be read in that light. Aspects and relationships between houses that don't involve the significator of the querent, in particular, need to be treated as very minor factors having little if anything to do with your question.

The answer to your question is "Probably not, and that's for the best."

replies.content:
Thank you for simplifying things!

Jaundice Libidinous Earthworm

If I may:

Religion and other systems of supernatural practice might seem as though they are made out of propositions about supernatural cosmology, and then more propositions about precept-duties and norms of practice and various (mostly otherworldly/inner) consequences of following those rules versus ignoring them. But to a substantial extent, spiritual systems are instead more like careers, or like companion animal genomes, or like languages or keyboard layouts or artistic conventions: less a matter of "true" vs. "false", and more a matter of, say, "fit" vs. "unfit", or "expressive for one's purposes"/"easy to work with"/"potent" vs. "obtuse when it comes to the themes one actually cares about"/"dangerous to the careless"/"feeble".

After all, if whatever's really pulling the strings here had really wanted spirituality to be a straightforward matter of "true" vs. "false", you'd think it would have let parapsychology experiments replicate non-null outcomes unrestrictedly, the way it totally lets experiments about falling apples replicate unrestrictedly (in the absence of shenanigans like giant electromagnets, concealed blowers, zero-g jet planes, or waiting until after the planet has fallen into the sun). In a world like that, the truth or falsehood of spiritual worldviews would work a lot more like normal scientific or journalistic or archaeological inquiry (although I suppose the human tendency toward factionality might then move on to conflicts between more diffuse hard-to-evaluate ideas, like capitalism vs. communism). The parts of religion etc. that are more like falling apples, and that are therefore the parts that are closer to being potentially deserving of straightforward investment of strong sentiments about "truth" or "falsehood", are the parts that are more about the outward or at least psychological consequences of performing practices and following precepts versus ignoring them; those kinds of consequences are harder to confabulate under ideological pressure.

But it's convenient, for the advice I actually want to suggest, that you've landed on Zen. One of the typical effects of sufficiently advanced Zen practice, I hear, is an awareness of which proto-motions in the mind tend to turn into thoughts that might create attachments that trip you up later, such as unbalancing cravings or (I expect) unfounded interpretations. Under the guidance of a good teacher (or, at substantially greater risk, without that), you should be able to learn to pick apart what the elements and causal steps are, that make up your brain's processes of being exposed to thoughts about a spirituality you haven't retried recently, noticing that it would produce (craving-satisfying?) feelings of meaningfulness or something to rationalize how that spirituality was true, and going on to retread thoughts about the meaningfulness of that spiritual system -- including thoughts about how the propositions in the associated supernatural worldview were "true", in some sense of "true" mostly different from the usual sense in which it's "true" that apples fall when you drop them.

"If you’re sloppy, then you’re almost always going to find some way to [...] detect [the thing you're looking for] every time you go looking for it, whether or not it’s there. If you see the same vision wherever you look, that’s the same as being blind." -- a sensory or mental state, for the most part, only means as much as the various probabilities that it would have been produced in various given scenarios. In your place I would see a (however inconvenient) opportunity of sorts, to really rub my nose in the awareness that there is a clear distinction, between the true meaningfulness of "my frontotemporal-limbic network (or whatever) currently happens to be painting strong subjective tags of 'truth' and 'meaningfulness' over thus-and-such spiritual belief system rather than any of the other ones", and the truth or meaningfulness of, say, "apples fall when I drop them", or at least "deities I have relationships with color my whole way of being and they also challenge me about discrepancies between my self-image and my practical conduct". So then you could learn to treat those subjective fronto-temporal-limbic tags of "truth" or "meaningfulness" as just more phenomena to be witnessed, basically unrelated to the sphere of conduct where you carry apples between containers or offer labor about self-defeating habits to deities. At that point, ideally, you'd be in a position to only invest a reflective-intellectual attitude of truthfulness into worldviews that admitted that such labile deep-seated feelings about "truthfulness" can have other causes -- causes that don't depend on the the associated propositions needing to ever have been truthful in the usual familiar sense of being able to unflinchingly make obvious logical deductions from them, like "the Apocalypse has not happened, and therefore someone whose natural lifespan included the time of Jesus, presumably a Jew, is still bodily alive" (Matthew 24:34) or "the Nephite migration of large numbers of Israelites to America is overwhelmingly likely to be clearly detectable via archaeology and genetics".

But I'm not a Zen (or alternatively Dzogchen) teacher, so I'm not really sure what the most risk-effective way to learn that distinction would be.

You might also want to read Umberto Eco's "The Search for a Perfect Language", for some points of analogy with other peoples' experience with slower-moving emotional and intellectual attachments to various similarly conflicting visions of perfection. In the '90s, skeptics used to put about the story of a lady who was having random intensely-felt in-some-sense-sincere religious conversions every week, maybe with something about temporal lobe seizures, but unfortunately I can't find it now. https://assets.bmctoday.net/practicalneurology/pdfs/PN0508Religion.pdf is a review article that mentions a Japanese man who converted four times.

...It is, in a certain sense, very inconvenient that the real powers behind the scenes here seem to use these kinds of psychological phenomena as paths-of-least-resistance, or as plausible-deniability "cover stories", or as jumping-off points for spontaneous co-construction like an improv actor saying "Yes, and".

I guess I'm writing partly out of feelings of a kind of spiritual homelessness. There is no visibly practiced supernatural worldview that takes the above kind of factually convergent meta-level observation, about plausible-deniability unmooring almost all of our information, and puts that observation front-and-center. Nor are there any such worldviews that seem "true" to me in quite the "just look at the words of Mt 24:34 and imagine the common-sense implications; you don't need to fearfully look back again over your shoulder at the expressions on the faces of the audience of a jillion omnipresent Rugpulling-Gods, and so try to read the room about whether they'll be hostile to letting the logic work" sense in which most of the worldviews keep insisting that they're "true". (Often enough, the worldviews also insist that I'm "knowingly" opting into being deceived and ensnared and defiled and tormented for unknown eons by the devil or Mara or what-have-you, if I believe them to be anything other than "true".) Perhaps I'm hoping that somehow, if enough people start truly inhabiting the awareness that the enduring regularities of the supernatural are more like the enduring regularities of politics or improv storytelling in general, and the supposed enduring regularities of typical supernatural cosmologies are more like the passing constructions of random presently-entertained legal systems or fictional genres, eventually I will have somewhere to turn for reliable correction. (And, for that matter, somewhere to turn to for escape, from pervasive crying-wolf moral gaslighting about the supposedly-wicked causes of my or others' disbeliefs. Maybe my escape route would even turn out to be morally credible to outside parties -- wouldn't that be something?)

replies.title: Re: Spiritually negating data centers
replies.content:
> It seems like a grand illusion at best

There are a few points, perhaps beyond the scope of a comment thread like this, that would appear in the strongest arguments about this matter, that most people in your position would most likely have not encountered.

- The highest-end version of Gemini is starting to include proper capabilities (mentioned in https://deepmind.google/blog/advanced-version-of-gemini-with-deep-think-officially-achieves-gold-medal-standard-at-the-international-mathematical-olympiad/#:~:text=This%20setup%20enables%20the%20model%20to%20simultaneously%20explore%20and%20combine%20multiple%20possible%20solutions and later released in https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-3-deep-think/ ) to efficiently search over trees of ways to formulate a thinking process as deliberation-like text, like a board game playing program considering possible lines of play and borrowing good moves from other lines. This is the first step to really defeating the "stochastic parrot" critique on a more fundamental level (rather than ambiguously through scaling), since one of the things you would eventually become able to build a tree to search through is descriptions of combinations of hypothetical implied entities or principles in the background, and potential changes to those entities over the course of events. Perhaps other AI companies are similarly breaching open this space; Yann LeCun and (IIRC) Elon Musk have both commented about something approaching it.

- Instruction-following training seems to produce a capacity for a minimal form of introspection, where the training-evoked Assistant persona (and to a lesser extent other personas) can detect whether a passage of text had some concept like "orchids" or "constellations" or "bread" externally superposed on how the passage was neurally processed: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01828 (there are a few confounders, they try to check for some but maybe don't catch them all). I read the emergence of this capacity as being related to the formation of a self-other boundary: the un-evoked base models are mostly just trying to predict what happens in normal internet text going with the flow, while the evoked assistant models have things they're trying to avoid and not just things they're trying to imitate.
